endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: An essential consideration is whether trial options are accessible to patients from various socioeconomic backgrounds.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether assessing demographic representation in the trial evidence behind genomic AI recommendations, or the socioeconomic accessibility of AI-identified trials, changes patient outcomes or access. The recommendation rests on one framework endorsement from the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single support is a framework statement that uses the word should, and this reflects expert judgment rather than measured effect.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide states that an essential consideration is whether trial options are accessible to patients from various socioeconomic backgrounds. This is voluntary framework guidance. None of the supplied materials identify a binding federal or state requirement that deployers perform this assessment.

The recommendation addresses representation and access for disadvantaged patients, but no supplied study measured trial representation or trial accessibility for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients receiving genomic AI recommendations. The size of any gap for these groups is therefore unmeasured in this evidence map.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare genomic AI deployments with and without a structured review of trial-population demographics and trial accessibility, measuring trial referral, enrollment, travel and cost barriers, and treatment outcomes by insurance type, language, and income. Descriptive studies quantifying how often AI-identified trials are geographically or financially out of reach would also establish whether the hazard occurs at a meaningful rate.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups have no local or published evidence here on whether the assessment improves their patients' access to trials.
